Research · supervised study, paper written

The answer everyone expects turned out to be wrong

Skin cancer apps work noticeably worse on darker skin. Almost everyone agrees why: the training photos are overwhelmingly of light skin, so the obvious fix is to add more images of darker skin. I ran a controlled study to test whether that fix actually works.

It did not. Adding real darker-skin photographs to the training data made the model worse on darker skin, not better, dropping its accuracy on healthy dark skin from 81% to 64%. I ran the same experiment with lighter-skin photos as a control, and that degraded too. So the problem was never really about who was in the photos.

The real problem is that the two sets of photos are different kinds of picture. The model learned from tight clinical close-ups of a single mole, but real people upload wider phone photos with skin and background around it. It is like training someone on passport photos and then asking them to identify faces in holiday snaps. Until that gap is closed, adding more diverse data cannot help, because the model cannot read either kind reliably.

This matters because it changes what you should spend effort on. Collecting more diverse images is slow, expensive and ethically delicate, and this study suggests it will not fix the problem on its own. The paper is written up in full with the method, the numbers and an honest list of what it does not prove.

Accuracy on healthy skin, by skin tone
ModelLightMediumDarkGap
Starting point78.6%84.4% 81.4%no real gap
After adding darker-skin photos76.9%77.8% 64.4%gap returns, 12.5 points
After adding lighter-skin photos (control)74.4% 83.8%71.2% also worse
